## OQ-1166 — Does a BASE-ONLY service get topped up to the minimum bill? (CR-052 W1, 2026-08-30)

**Type:** finance · **Source:** BR-RAT-028 as built (CR-052 tasks 4–7) · **Blocks:** nothing — the rule is implemented as written and this asks whether an exception belongs in it · **Status:** ✅ **CLOSED 2026-08-30 — option (b). BUILT 2026-08-31.**

⚠ **THIS ROW READ `Status: OPEN` FOR A DAY AFTER IT WAS ANSWERED, AND THE CODE HELD THE OPTION THE PO RULED AGAINST.** The ruling was recorded in `12-governance/02-decision-log.md` on 2026-08-30 under the heading *“A MINIMUM IS ABOUT USAGE SOMEBODY WAS SUPPOSED TO USE”*, which states in its own words that this row is answered and that its `$42.00` *“should never have been charged”*. It reached this registry and `apply_charges.py` on 2026-08-31. That is r11 step 0's named failure mode — a ruling that reaches every document and not the code — and it is recorded here rather than tidied away.

**PO ruling, verbatim (2026-08-30):**

> *“when units are vacant - at that time, we are only charging base rates. minimum rates are applied when consumer is suppose to use minimum usage, but they end up using less than what they are suppose ot use”*

**THE ANSWER IS (b), and the general test the PO gave is the useful part:** *a minimum applies when a consumer was SUPPOSED to use a minimum and used less.* A vacant unit was not supposed to use anything, so there is nothing to fall short of. A vacation hold is the same customer one service at a time.

**BUILT 2026-08-31.** `apply_charges.minimum_adjustment_line` takes `base_only` and returns None for it; `engine.price_bill` — the only caller that knows the flag — hands it down. Six empty units at an `$8.00` water base under a `$15.00` per-service minimum now price `$48.00` instead of `$90.00`: **`$42.00` a month off that owner's bill**, which is this row's own figure. Proved in `06-backend/tests/test_cr052_w0_task2_vacant_is_not_free.py` (8 cases), whose guard was shown RED first on the pre-ruling behaviour — `AssertionError: Left contains one more item: RatedLine(kind='minimum_adjustment', … amount=Decimal('7.00'), … service='water')`.

❄️ **NO FROZEN FIGURE MOVED, MEASURED NOT ASSUMED.** `WE-3`/`GT-19` is a METERED water household at `0.4 kgal` — it prices a usage line, so it is not base-only and cannot reach the new branch. `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` reads **33 PASS / 0 FAIL** before and after, and the case is re-priced inside the new test file so the claim is a measurement rather than a commit message.

⚠ **TWO THINGS THIS CLOSURE DOES NOT COVER, BOTH FILED RATHER THAN GUESSED.** **Mode B — the PLAN FLOOR** applied once over the whole finished bill — still tops up a bill made entirely of vacant units (`8.00` of base under a `40.00` floor is still `40.00`): `DEF-2822`, because this row costed the PER-SERVICE minimum and that is the figure the PO worked. And the **minimum-USAGE half** of the same ruling — a minimum QUANTITY rather than a minimum amount — is a new column and needs the four things the decision log lists as owed, none of which is taken here.

**The rule that is now live.** BR-RAT-028 is CONFIRMED and says a minimum bill
is charged per service and, on top of that, per plan. It was signed weeks ago and
had never been built, because the two amounts a clerk types — the per-service
minimum on the plan, and the plan floor — could not travel to the pricing engine.
They travel now, and the engine tops a short service up to its minimum. On the
signed example, a water-only household using 0.4 kgal is charged 1.60 of usage
plus 8.00 of base = 9.60, and a 15.00 minimum adds a **5.40** line called
"Minimum bill adjustment"; with tax the bill is **$16.42**.

**The question, in plain English.** Some services on a bill are charged their
base and nothing else, on purpose — a customer on a vacation hold, and every
empty unit on a landlord's building, whose base charges land on the owner's bill.
BR-RAT-028 does not say whether those should ALSO be topped up to the minimum,
and the rule as written contains no exception, so the code applies it to them
like any other service and this row records the consequence rather than an
invented exemption.

**What it costs, worked.** On the building the rules use as their standing
example, six empty units each take water at an `$8.00` base. Under a `$15.00`
per-service minimum each one is topped up by `$7.00`, so the owner is charged
**`$42.00` a month more** for units nobody lives in. A customer on a vacation
hold is in the same position one service at a time.

**The two answers.**

* **(a) Top them up, as today.** The minimum is what the utility charges to keep
  a connection available, and an empty unit still has one. Nothing changes; this
  row closes.
* **(b) Exempt a base-only service from the minimum.** A hold and an empty unit
  are exactly the cases where the customer has been told they are paying the
  base and no more, so a minimum that quietly raises it reads as a broken
  promise. One line of code, and `$42.00` a month comes off that owner's bill.

~~**Implemented as (a) — the rule as signed — and flagged.**~~ **SUPERSEDED 2026-08-31 — the PO ruled (b) on 2026-08-30 and the code was moved to (b).** The struck sentence is kept because a reader who greps for it must find out what happened to it (hard-won law 1). `apps/rating/pricing/stages/apply_charges.py` still names this row and now states the ruling instead of the question.

## OQ-1221 — A service the utility has never priced a standing charge for: does the bill print a `$0.00` line, or no line? (`DEF-2864`, 2026-08-31)

**Type:** finance · **Source:** the PO's own bill BL-2608-000048 · **Blocks:** `DEF-2864` only — nothing else is waiting on it, and no figure moves either way · **Status:** ⚖️ **CLOSED 2026-08-31 — PO RULING, OPTION (a): LEAVE IT AS IT IS.**

⚖️ **THE RULING.** Put to the PO in plain English with the figure — *a line reading `sewer base charge — 0.00 USD` for something nobody ever charged for, two of the ten services configured that way, no money moving either way* — together with the fact that option (b) would reverse their own ruling of 2026-08-19. **They chose (a): leave it.**

**SO THE 2026-08-19 RULING STANDS AND IS NOW RULED TWICE.** *"A zero means it is free and the bill prints `$0.00`"* is the behaviour, deliberately, on a second look with the consequence in front of them. `DEF-2864` closes as RULED BEHAVIOUR and not as a defect.

**AND OPTION (c) IS DECLINED BY IMPLICATION, WRITTEN DOWN RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE RE-ASKED (law 13):** there is no new column, no third state in the price book, and no migration over the zeros already stored. A lane proposing any of those is reversing a decision, not finishing a stub.

**The question, in plain English.** The PO's bill carries a line reading
**`sewer base charge   —   —   0.00 USD`**. Nobody set a standing charge for
sewer: our own configuration writes a zero there, and the comment beside it says
in as many words that the price book *"names one for electric and water and none
for sewer"*. So the customer is shown a charge line for something the utility
never charged for.

**Why it cannot simply be deleted.** Today the product understands two answers
and needs a third:

* **a blank** means *this service is not available at this size* and the bill
  STOPS, so the customer gets no bill at all. That is CR-013 part 1, ruled
  2026-08-19.
* **a zero** means *it is free* and the bill prints `$0.00`. That is the PO's own
  ruling of the same day, in the words **"print $0.00"**, taken so that rows
  already in the database — where nobody could tell "free" from "not available"
  apart — would go on billing instead of failing.
* **there is no way to say *this service simply has no standing charge***, which
  is what is actually true of sewer, so the configuration writes a zero and the
  zero prints a line.

**What it costs, worked.** Nothing, in money — the line is `$0.00` and every
total is identical either way. What it costs is trust in the paper: two of the
ten services this product ships (sewer and trash) are configured exactly like
this, so a customer on both reads two charge lines for two things that were never
charged, on the same page as the charges that are real.

**The three answers.**

* **(a) Leave it.** A zero line is a complete statement — *we looked at sewer and
  charged you nothing for it* — and it is what the 2026-08-19 ruling said to do.
  Nothing changes and this row closes.
* **(b) Print no line for a standing charge of zero.** One line of code in the
  pricing engine, no money moves, and the bill shows only what was charged.
  **This REVERSES part of the 2026-08-19 ruling** — that ruling was shown
  exactly these two options and chose the printed zero — so it needs the PO to
  say so, which is why this is a question and not a decision we took.
* **(c) Give the configuration a way to say "this service has no standing
  charge"**, separate from "free" and from "not available", and set it for sewer
  and trash. This is the honest answer and the expensive one: a new column, a
  control on the plan's services screen and on the charge-code screen, and a
  migration decision about every zero already stored.

**What was NOT done here, and why.** The pricing path was left exactly as it is.
Reversing a signed ruling by choosing (b) on our own is the one thing CLAUDE.md
law 13 sends to the PO rather than deciding, and picking (c) silently would put a
column in the schema on our own judgment. `DEF-2864` carries the defect;
`12-governance/02-decision-log.md` (2026-08-31) carries the full mechanism, so
whoever answers this does not have to find it again.

## OQ-1252 — A property is sold. What happens to the money the seller still owes? (`CR-058` W4, 2026-09-01)

**Type:** finance · **Source:** PO ruling 2026-09-01, *"dont create new account - we reassing that account - bascailly I have sold my property - so account get transfer to new person or business"* · **Blocks:** nothing — it was answered inside the hour it was raised · **Status:** ⚖️ **CLOSED 2026-09-01 — PO RULING: THE DEBT FOLLOWS THE PROPERTY.**

⚖️ **THE RULING, VERBATIM:** *"money follow property - new owner boutght everything property + debt also"*. **When a property is sold, the outstanding balance goes with it. The buyer takes the property and the debt.** Recorded in full in `12-governance/02-decision-log.md`, 2026-09-01, *"THREE MORE RULINGS…"* §3. **It must not be re-asked (law 13).**

**AND IT MADE THE BUILD SMALLER RATHER THAN BIGGER, WHICH IS WORTH RECORDING.** The PO ruled in the same exchange that a transfer **REASSIGNS the same account**. An account carries its own ledger, so reassigning the account **is** the debt following the property: **the balance never moves, because the thing it sits on never moves.** The buyer becomes the customer of an account that already owes what it owes. Had transfer stayed as built — a new account at a new unit — this ruling would have required lifting a balance off one account and posting it onto another, which is a debt transfer between two parties and needs its own money path, its own audit and probably its own consent.

**WHAT WAS BUILT.** `apps/customers/transfers.py::reassign_account` moves the customer and **writes no journal line, raises no refund and touches no `deposit_on_file` or `balance`**. The balance and the deposit AS THEY STOOD at the moment of sale are recorded on the audit row and returned to the caller — the figure the buyer is taking on, stated rather than silent.

**WHAT IT DID NOT LICENCE, and the stub that was written for this row was deleted rather than repurposed.** Hard rule 4 stands: invoices, invoice lines, payments and journal entries already issued to the SELLER stay exactly as issued, in the seller's name, for ever. A bill posted to a named person is a record of what was sent, not a statement of who owes it today.

**The three answers this row originally offered** — (a) the debt stays with the seller, (b) the debt follows the property, (c) the sale is refused until the balance is zero — are kept for the record. **The PO chose (b).** (a) and (c) are DECLINED and a lane proposing either is reversing a ruling, not finishing a stub.

## OQ-1253 — Must the buyer be SHOWN the debt they are taking on, and where? (`CR-058` W4, 2026-09-01)

**Type:** product · **Source:** raised by the lane building the reassignment, from the PO's own ruling of 2026-09-01 (*"money follow property - new owner boutght everything property + debt also"*), which answers where the money goes and says nothing about who is told · **Blocks:** nothing — the reassignment is built and works · **Status:** 🔴 **OPEN — not answered by inference.**

**The question, in plain English.** Mr Okafor buys 1408 Elm Street. The account moves to him and **$284.60 of unpaid charges move with it** — that is ruled and it is not in question here. **What nobody has said is whether he has to be shown that figure before it becomes his, and if so, where.** Being sold a property with arrears attached is a thing most people would expect to see in writing.

**Why it is a real question and not tidiness.** Today the clerk performing the reassignment is shown the balance and the deposit as they stand, and the audit row records both. **The buyer is shown nothing** — the product has no document, no screen and no acknowledgement addressed to him at the moment of sale. He finds out when the next bill arrives with a balance brought forward that predates him.

**The options, with what each costs.**

* **(a) Nothing.** The property sale is a private transaction between two people and the utility's job is to bill whoever owns the account. Costs nothing to build; the buyer's first notice of the debt is his first bill.
* **(b) The clerk must confirm it, on screen, with the figure.** One confirmation step in the reassignment: *"this account owes $284.60. It moves to the new owner."* Cheap, and it puts the fact in front of a human being before the act — but the human is the clerk, not the buyer.
* **(c) The buyer is sent a document.** A statement of what the account owes at the moment it becomes theirs, through the notifications module like any other document. This is what *"in writing"* actually means, and it is the most work: a template, a trigger and a delivery record.
* **(d) The buyer must acknowledge it before the reassignment completes.** The strongest, and it makes the sale un-recordable until somebody replies — which a clerk standing at a counter cannot always wait for.

**What is built while this is open, and it is not a stub.** The reassignment WORKS and the ruling is fully implemented: the debt follows the property. The response and the audit row both carry `balance_at_sale` and `deposit_at_sale`, so whichever answer arrives, **the figure is already computed at the right moment and nothing has to be reconstructed afterwards.** Option (a) needs no further work at all; (b), (c) and (d) each consume that figure.

## OQ-1322 — How is a payment's cheque number corrected, when the row may never be updated? (`CR-059` CS-34, 2026-09-02)

**Raised by:** the `CR-059` W7 lane, building task 41.
**Status:** OPEN — blocking CS-34's write half. Everything else in CS-34 is built.

### The question in one sentence

A clerk types `10241` on a cheque that says `10214`. Nothing financial is wrong — the
amount, the account and both dates are right — but the bank statement will never match,
and there is no way in this product to fix the number. **CS-34 says the reference and the
memo may be amended. CLAUDE.md hard rule 4 says a payment may never be updated. Both are
signed, and nothing on the record says which one gives way.**

### Why it is not a lane's call

`CR-059` §2 exists precisely for this: it lists **thirteen** signed statements this change
request reverses, with the supersession stated for each. Hard rule 4 is not among them.
CLAUDE.md law 13 puts *"a ruling that collides with a signed rule — the supersession must
be stated, never assumed"* on the Product Owner's list.

And the rule is not a convention. `apps/payments/migrations/0002_rls_w4_and_immutability.py`
installs `payments_payment_immutable()`:

    psycopg.errors.RaiseException: BR-PAY-002 / hard rule 4: payment PY-260808-0001 is
      cleared and is append-only — no column may change except the deposit batch it is
      banked in (BR-PAY-025) and the journal entry it posted (US-PAY-009), each once.
      A reversal, an NSF and a reapply are all NEW rows. Changed: confirmation
    CONTEXT: PL/pgSQL function payments_payment_immutable() line 23 at RAISE

— **quoted from a real PostgreSQL run, not read off a migration.** ⚠ The live body is
`payments/0006`, not `0002`: 0005 and 0006 each replaced the function, which is why the
message names two write-once stamps 0002 has never heard of. Past `processing` a payment
may GAIN `deposit_batch_id` and `journal_entry_id`, each exactly once; while still
`processing` it may move `status` and `cleared_at`. **`confirmation` (the cheque number),
`memo` and `method_id` (the tender) are outside BOTH lists**, and everything absent from
them — including every column added after the migration — is frozen by whole-row
comparison.

⚠ **AND THE NAIVE FIX WOULD HAVE SHIPPED GREEN.** Those triggers are installed on
**PostgreSQL only** — the migration's own docstring says so — and `config/settings/test.py`
hardcodes in-memory SQLite. So `Payment.objects.filter(pk=…).update(confirmation=…)` passes
every test in this repository, on every machine, and raises the first time a real clerk
corrects a real cheque. That is CLAUDE.md law 14 exactly, one module along from where it
was learned. `tests/test_cr059_cs34_amend_reference.py` records the limit in a case of its
own rather than leaving it to be discovered.

### The three readings

**(a) Widen the trigger's allow list.** Add `confirmation`, `memo` and `method_id` to
`mutable`, in every status. It is the cheapest answer and it is exactly the screen CS-34
draws: S21 shows the row's own corrected value and hovers the previous one from the audit
trail. **The cost is that *"no column may change"* stops being true of `payments`** — the
sentence `CR-059` §7 uses to describe the module's central guarantee — **and the previous
value then lives ONLY in `audit_log`, which this product prunes on a retention schedule.**
So a customer ringing about a cheque number from two years ago becomes unfindable by
design, which is the opposite of what CS-34's own screen note asks for.

**(b) A new append-only `payment_amendments` table.** The correction is a NEW ROW, which is
what hard rule 4 says a correction is, and the history is permanent and queryable rather
than living in a log with a retention policy. It costs a table CS-34's own *"Data. None."*
says it does not need, and **every reader that matches on a reference has to read through
it** — bank auto-match, and the S33 search at `apps/payments/selectors.py:314`, which
matches `confirmation__icontains`. A reader that did not would go on matching the wrong
value, silently.

**(c) Correct by reversal, which already works.** Reverse the payment and record it again
with the right reference. Nothing new is built at all. It writes three payment rows and two
journal entries to fix a typo, and it moves the money through the books twice — which is
the disproportion CS-34 was written to remove.

### What is built while this is open — and it is most of the spec

`apps/payments/amendments.py` + `amendments_api.py`, mounted at
`POST /payments/{id}/correct-reference`:

* **the NAMED endpoint, deliberately not a PATCH** — CS-34's own reason, verbatim: *"a
  route that accepts a partial body invites the next field to be added to it"*. No PATCH,
  PUT or DELETE is added to any payment path;
* **every money field refused BY NAME** — CS-34's first proof, live today. A body carrying
  `amount`, `account_id`, `posted_at`, `cleared_at` or `allocations` is refused with that
  field named, before the payment is even looked up;
* **the tender refused once the payment is in a deposit batch** — CS-34's second new rule,
  which needs no write to be true. The refusal names the batch (`DEP-260808-CHK`, the label,
  never its id) and says something DIFFERENT for a reconciled batch, because unreconciling
  and re-cutting are different acts;
* **the required note**, and an unknown field refused rather than ignored;
* **the audit row's SHAPE**, composed and asserted, carrying the old value and the new — so
  whichever reading wins, hard rule 7's evidence half is already decided and identical.

**Only the write raises `NotImplementedError`.** It refuses nothing that works today,
because nothing corrects a reference today — so this is the `OQ-204`/S74 posture and not
`OQ-500`'s, where a stub would have refused to open an account in order to ask a question.

⚠ **`CR-059` task 42 (S35's modal, S21's corrected-value hover) must render its control
DISABLED WITH THIS REASON** (`BR-SHL-025`), not wire a form to the stub.


## OQ-1360 — and the one thing already decided under it: the hydrant's NAME

⚠⚠ **DISSOLVED 2026-09-03 — THE ROW THIS SECTION IS ABOUT NO LONGER EXISTS, AND THAT IS NOT
THE SAME AS THE QUESTION BEING ANSWERED.** PO 2026-09-03: *"remove private hydrants from
list"*. `HYD` has left fire's size list, so there is no seeded name left to tighten and
`DEF-3090`'s hand-off to the `CR-063` lane is discharged by the row's withdrawal rather than
by a naming convention. **`test_cr039_e21_service_size_classes.UNPREFIXED_BY_RECORD` no longer
carries `HYD`**, and it must not be re-added: a register of divergences that lists a code the
product does not seed is a register that cannot fail on the real thing.

**WHY THE REASONING BELOW IS KEPT RATHER THAN DELETED, and it is the useful half.** Point 2 is
a live, general rule that outlives this row — a seeded name is not free to change, `BR-TEN-072`
forbids the rename and `BR-TEN-071` makes it pointless — and `G-250` is still the standing
precedent for it. Point 1's argument (*don't rename a row that is about to be superseded*) is
now the argument for not renaming the SIX that remain, which is exactly what it always was.
**Read what follows as the standing rule with its one worked example withdrawn.**

⚠ **`DEF-3090` HANDS THE RENAME OF `HYD` TO THE `CR-063` LANE *"with `OQ-1360`"*, AND THIS IS
THAT LANE ANSWERING IT — WITH A DECISION, NOT A DEFERRAL.**

`HYD` is seeded as **"Private hydrant"**, which does not name its service; fire's other six read
*"Fire line 2\""* and do. `BR-TEN-078` leaves this list unscoped, so a row's own name is the only
thing that says which service it belongs to — which makes the divergence real rather than
cosmetic. **It waits on this question deliberately, and the reasons are recorded so nobody
re-opens it as an oversight.**

**1 · THIS ANSWER REPLACES ALL SEVEN ROWS WHOLESALE.** The going-live customer types their own
size list. Renaming one row now renames a row that is about to be superseded, and the customer's
names will need the naming convention applied to all of them at once rather than to one.

**2 · A SEEDED NAME IS NOT FREE TO CHANGE, AND THIS REPO HAS ALREADY RULED ON THE IDENTICAL
CASE.** `BR-TEN-072` forbids a rename in seed data and `BR-TEN-071` makes one pointless for any
tenant that already holds the row. That is exactly why `G-250` still reads *"Gas 250 CFH
(residential)"* although the ratified table says a bare *"250 CFH"*: `service_size_classes.py`
says in terms that tightening a shipped name *"would be a rename, which BR-TEN-072 forbids in seed
data and BR-TEN-071 makes pointless anyway"*. **Tightening `HYD` unilaterally would be doing the
thing that precedent declined.**

**SO THE ANSWER TO THIS QUESTION SETTLED THE HYDRANT'S NAME TOO — and then the PO removed the
row instead (2026-09-03), which settles it a different way and settles nothing about the six
that remain.** While `HYD` was seeded,
`test_cr039_e21_service_size_classes.UNPREFIXED_BY_RECORD` carried it **by defect id rather than
by approval** — a sibling lane's design, and the thing that stopped it quietly becoming
permanent. It has been taken out of that register with the row itself.
Storm water's five sit in the same register and are the opposite case: those names ARE approved,
the PO was shown them as they read, and reversing them needs the PO because the names are theirs.

## OQ-RAT-1766 — Does a plan's `late_fee_pct` / `late_fee_min` still override the charge code? (`CR-078`, 2026-09-07)

**STATUS: OPEN.** Raised by the lane that built `CR-078`, and deliberately NOT answered by it.

**WHAT CHANGED UNDER IT.** `BR-RAT-1011` (PO 2026-09-07, finance re-signed) makes the late
fee's percent and minimum come from the charge code the PLAN names, and makes a plan naming
none charge **$0.00**. Before that ruling those two figures came from Settings → Billing
defaults, with an optional per-plan override on `plan_penalty_rules.late_fee_pct` /
`late_fee_min`, every NULL falling back to the tenant.

**THE QUESTION, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** A utility can already type a late-fee percentage and a
minimum on the plan itself. It can now also point the plan at a charge code that carries a
percentage and a minimum. **If both are filled in, which one does the bill use?** Three
answers are defensible and only the PO can pick:

  * **(a) The charge code, always.** The typed figures become dead columns and should be taken
    off the screen, because a control that changes nothing is worse than no control.
  * **(b) The typed figures win where they are filled in**, and the charge code is what a plan
    falls back to. That keeps both features and makes the plan's own numbers an override of the
    code rather than of the tenant.
  * **(c) The typed figures are retired** — the utility edits the charge code instead, which is
    where every other fee's amount already lives (`BR-BIL-007`).

**WHAT THE PRODUCT DOES TODAY, AND WHY THAT IS NOT AN ANSWER.** Reading (a): the fee path
(`late_fee.assess_late_fee_for_plan`) reads only the charge code, because that is what the
ruling says word for word. **The two columns are still written by the plan editor and still
read by `plan_detail` and the unit pricing panel**, so a clerk can type a figure that changes
no bill — which is exactly the *live screen behind a dead control* shape CLAUDE.md's hard-won
law 2 records, and it is the reason this question cannot simply be left.

**WHY IT WAS NOT DECIDED HERE.** The finance re-sign of 2026-09-07 lists four decisions it
covers and says, in its own words, that *"a later lane finding a fifth decision here must
return to the agenda rather than read it as covered"*. This is that fifth decision, and it
moves money: on a plan typed at 2% against a `LATE` code at 1.5%, a $5,247.31 overdue balance
is **$104.95** under reading (b) and **$78.71** under reading (a) — a **$26.24** difference per
late bill.

**NOT AFFECTED, so nobody need re-open it:** the GRACE half (`grace_days`, `grace_mode`) is
untouched by `CR-078` and still falls back to the tenant's own settings (`BR-BIL-008`,
`BR-BIL-002`).

## OQ-RAT-12347 — Seven sewer figures moved and only six were signed: WE-6/GT-22, and the payments/ledger workbooks that consume WE-1's total (`CR-081`, 2026-09-08)

**STATUS: OPEN.** Raised by the lane that built `CR-081` and deliberately NOT answered by it.
Nothing is blocked: the product ships and every signed figure is correct. What is open is
whether a handful of OTHER ❄️ frozen numbers should follow.

**WHAT HAPPENED, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** You re-signed six sewer amounts on 2026-09-08 — the
reference bill and four others — and the code, the tests and the workbook now all agree with
them. While doing that we found a **seventh sewer amount on a sixth example** that was never
put in front of you, and a set of **later examples that use the reference bill's total as
their starting number**. A signature covers only what was shown, so none of those has been
touched.

**THE SEVENTH FIGURE.** `WE-6` is the "first bill" example — a customer who moves in on the
12th, so everything prorates. Its sewer line reads **$7.69** today. On the rule you signed it
would be 90% of 4.2 thousand gallons at $5.00 = **$18.90**, which would take that bill's
taxable amount from **$102.53** to **$113.74** and its total from **$287.23** to **$299.49**.

**THE LATER EXAMPLES.** The reference bill's total moved from **$292.87** to **$314.97**, a
difference of **$22.10**. Five payments examples and the finance trial balance start from that
$292.87 and were signed with it: the outstanding-balance example, two allocation examples, the
bounced-cheque example, the deposit-batch example and the month-end trial balance. The vacation
-hold bill moved by **$9.84** the same way. Every one of them still adds up correctly against
its own workbook; they simply start from yesterday's number.

**WHY WE DID NOT JUST FIX THEM.** Changing a signed figure needs your signature, and you were
not shown these. Fixing them quietly would have been us deciding what you meant.

**WHAT WE DID INSTEAD.** `10-scripts/03-golden-verify.py` now has a **Part 4** that recomputes
every one of these BOTH ways on every run and asserts the gap. It is counted separately from
the 33 signed checks, and it goes red the moment somebody moves one of them in either
direction — so the gap cannot be closed by accident while it is with you.

**THE CHOICE.**

  * **(a) Move them all**, on the same rule, and re-sign the set. Seven document figures plus
    the totals that follow; the code does not change at all.
  * **(b) Move only `WE-6`** (it is a sewer line, so it is the same ruling) and leave the
    payments and ledger examples alone as historical illustrations that name their date.
  * **(c) Leave everything as it is** and add a dated note to each saying it predates
    `CR-081`. Cheapest, and it means the workbook holds two eras side by side.

**Our recommendation is (a)**, because a workbook a clerk reads end to end should not price the
same service two ways — but it is the largest number of frozen figures to re-sign in one go and
it is genuinely your call. **Nothing is waiting on this**; the answer changes documents, not
code.

## OQ-CUS-1810 — what is the statutory period between a final disconnection notice and the earliest lawful cut, and how is it rolled past weekends and public holidays?

**Status: OPEN — BLOCKING screen 12 (the disconnect wizard, `S90`), and it is the
reason that screen carries the blueprint's only `BLOCKED` chip.**

**This question has been named in code three times and has never had an id.** It is
minted here rather than answered, and nothing below chooses a value.

### Where it is already written down, and where it is not

`07-frontend/src/features/customers/DisconnectWizard.tsx:1003` renders it to the
clerk, verbatim:

> *"The earliest lawful cut date is not computed anywhere in this product. It is
> the notice date plus the statutory period, rolled forward past weekends and
> public holidays, and nothing performs that roll — so this screen cannot show it
> and cannot stop an unlawful date being chosen here."*

`06-backend/apps/customers/transfer_disconnect_api.py:88` says the same of the
server — *"It computes no date… `cut_on` is the caller's"* — and the same file's
`E3` exception block says, in its own words, that *"a rule id for the
weekend/holiday roll does not exist in any signed document; REPORTED as a question
owed rather than minted here."*

⚠ **It was never minted.** Measured 2026-09-12: no row and no section of this
register names it, and `12-governance/02-decision-log.md` does not either. That is
hard-won law 1 exactly — *a comment claiming a plan is not the plan* — and it means
the one thing standing between a clerk and an unlawful cut has had no route to the
PO for as long as the screen has existed.

### What is actually built today, measured rather than described

Walked in Chromium at 1280 on 2026-09-12 against a private stack
(`10-scripts/cr094_lane4_ending_service_walkthrough.mjs`), on `A-11812`:

* step 3 renders the refusal above and then offers `Scheduled cut date *` as a
  **native `input[type="date"]` with NO `min` attribute** — measured on the element,
  not read from source. **Any date can be typed, including one before the notice.**
* its help text says so out loud: *"Check it against the statutory period yourself
  — this screen has no floor to check it against."*
* nothing downstream refuses either: the blueprint's own summary of this screen is
  *"a cut that nothing performs on the day it is scheduled for"*, and
  `GET /accounts/{id}/ladder` answers, in the server's own words,
  *"no runner, job, queue or timer in this product reads a date and acts on it"*
  (tracked as `DEF-320`).

### What an answer has to contain, and why one option cannot simply be picked

Three separate things, and only the first looks like a number:

1. **The period itself**, per tier. `A19 §2`'s three signed notice bodies name
   *10-day*, *5-day* and *48-hour* in their own prose, so a period per tier is
   already implied by signed copy — but no signed rule says the cut is counted from
   the final notice by any of them, and `OQ-377`'s body works its example on a
   **48 hour** period taken from `B18`'s fixture rather than from a rule.
2. **What the clock counts.** Calendar days, business days, or hours. These give
   different answers on the same case and the difference is a household's supply.
3. **Which calendar the roll uses.** Weekends are common ground; *public holidays*
   are per jurisdiction, and this product holds no holiday calendar for any tenant.
   A roll needs one, and where it comes from — platform default, per tenant, per
   regulator — is part of the answer rather than a detail of it.

⚠ **THE TRAP THAT MAKES THIS WORTH ASKING RATHER THAN INFERRING, AND THE CODE
ALREADY NAMES IT.** `DisconnectWizard.tsx`'s `E3` records that adding 48 hours would
implement *"+2 days"*, which **agrees with `B18`'s fixture by luck** — Aug 22 2026 is
a Saturday and Aug 24 the Monday, so the drawn case needs no roll at all and a wrong
implementation passes it. The blueprint's own step 3 draws *Earliest lawful cut
05/14/2026 · Counted from The final notice, 05/09/2026* — five days apart — and
**B14 rule 37 makes every figure drawn in a wireframe an illustration and never a
fact to build to**, so that pair is not evidence of a five-day rule and must not be
read as one. `ACC-S10`'s *what done looks like on screen* quotes that same drawn
date, which is the same hazard one document further on.

### Who can answer it

⚠ **THE PO, AND ONLY THE PO — this is law 13's third case, a fact only they hold.**
It is a regulator's rule in the jurisdictions this product serves, it is not
derivable from anything in this repository, and a lane choosing a period would be
choosing when a household's water goes off.

### What is built while this is open, stated so nobody "fixes" it quietly

The screen states the absence, offers no floor, and **refuses nothing** — which is
deliberate and is the honest position while the rule is unknown: a floor invented
here would be a different rule that happens to agree with the fixture. The date is
the clerk's and the screen says so. **A later lane must not add a `min` to
`dsc_cut_on` until this is answered**, and if a test ever asserts a computed
earliest date, it must be because the PO ruled and not because a bound looked safer.

**Raised:** 2026-09-12 by `CR-094-BRC01` step 1 lane 4 (ending service) ·
**Cites:** `DisconnectWizard.tsx:1003` and its `E3` block ·
`transfer_disconnect_api.py:88` · `A19 §2` · `OQ-377` · `OQ-382`–`OQ-385` ·
`DEF-320` · `ACC-S10` of `05-prototype/02 Accounts Menu Blueprint.pdf` ·
B14 rule 37 · hard-won law 1

## OQ-CUS-12350 — when a clerk corrects a customer's email, should their portal sign-in follow it? (`BR-CUS-1054`, 2026-09-13)

**STATUS: CLOSED 2026-10-22 — the clerk chooses.** PO, verbatim: *"give option to clark to make it log in email also if they choose it make login and bill email sent otherwise keep them separate"*; read back and confirmed, *"Your understanding is correct"*. Built (lane SIGNIN-EMAIL, `DEF-CWP-10400`): a tick box *"Also use this as the portal sign-in email"*, unticked by default, shown only when the customer has a portal login; ticked, the login moves too, the old address is told and a reset link goes to the new one. Decision log 2026-10-22, *"Who moves the portal sign-in email…"* and *"…built: the judgments"*. **⚠ THE BODY BELOW IS THE QUESTION AS IT WAS PUT ON 2026-09-13 AND DESCRIBES THE OPEN WORLD; it is kept, not followed.**

**STATUS AS PUT: OPEN.** Nothing is blocked. The customer edit ships and the email correction
works; what is open is whether a SECOND thing should happen at the same moment.

**WHAT HAPPENS TODAY, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** A clerk can now fix a customer's email address,
and that fix reaches every account that customer holds — so every future bill goes to the
right place. What it does NOT do is change the email address the customer types in to sign
in to the online portal. Those are two different addresses stored in two different places,
and today only the first one moves.

**WHY WE DID NOT JUST MAKE THEM FOLLOW EACH OTHER.** Both possible answers do harm if we
pick the wrong one, and neither is reversible by a clerk:

* **If the sign-in follows automatically:** a customer whose email a clerk corrects at the
  counter can no longer sign in with the address they have always used, and nobody tells
  them. If the clerk typed the new address wrongly, the account is now reachable by
  whoever owns that address.
* **If the sign-in never follows:** a customer who tells us their email changed keeps
  signing in with an address that no longer reaches them — so the *"we have emailed you a
  link"* half of a forgotten password goes nowhere, and the account becomes unrecoverable.

**THE THIRD OPTION, AND OUR RECOMMENDATION IF YOU WANT ONE.** Neither of the above: the
save says out loud that the sign-in has not moved, and offers the clerk a separate,
deliberate act to move it — one the customer confirms from the old address first. That
keeps a money-and-access change a decision somebody made rather than a side effect.

**WHAT IS BUILT MEANWHILE, so nobody "fixes" it quietly.** The correction writes the
billing contact and **nothing else**, the dialog says *"Portal sign-in does not move."* on
screen, and `test_correcting_the_email_does_not_move_the_portal_sign_in` fails if a later
lane makes it follow. There is also a rule reason: the sign-in lives in another module's
table and one module may not write another's (B2 §2), so linking the two is a new door
rather than a line of code.

**Raised:** 2026-09-13 by the `BR-CUS-1054` build lane ·
**Cites:** `apps/customers/customer_edit.py` · `apps/portal/models.PortalCredential`
(`ux_portal_credential_tenant_email`) · `apps/portal/credentials.normalise_email` ·
`BR-CWP-004` · B2 §2 · CLAUDE.md hard rule 7

## OQ-CUS-12351 — how does a customer filed as the wrong kind get corrected? (`BR-CUS-1054`, 2026-09-13)

**STATUS: OPEN.** Nothing is blocked. The edit refuses the change and says so; what is
open is what the right correction looks like.

**WHAT HAPPENS TODAY, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** Every customer is either a **person** or a
**company**, and the two are asked for different proof of identity: a person gives a Social
Security number, a driving licence or a phone; a company gives its Tax ID. If a clerk files
a business as a person by mistake, the new edit screen will not let anyone switch it over —
it refuses and names the reason.

**WHY IT REFUSES RATHER THAN JUST SWITCHING.** The proof already on file is stored in
columns that only that kind's matching rules ever look at. Flip a customer from person to
company and their Social Security number stays on the row, invisible, and nothing will ever
match on it again — so a returning customer stops being recognised and the **$150.00**
deposit that recognition carries stops following them. The row would look corrected and be
quietly broken, which is worse than a refusal.

**WHAT AN ANSWER HAS TO SAY.** Three things, and only the first looks like a yes or no:

1. **Is switching the kind allowed at all**, or is the answer *open the right one and close
   the wrong one*?
2. **What happens to the proof already on file** — cleared, kept, or the clerk asked to
   re-enter it in the right place.
3. **What happens to any account links and any deposit** that were made on the strength of
   the old proof, since those were judgments a human committed at a counter.

**WHAT IS BUILT MEANWHILE.** `kind` is refused by name with its reason, on the server, so
no door anywhere can flip it as a side effect. Nothing is lost: the customer record still
opens, still bills and still links.

**Raised:** 2026-09-13 by the `BR-CUS-1054` build lane ·
**Cites:** `BR-CUS-1022` (PO 2026-09-01) · `BR-CUS-089` (PO 2026-08-25, closing `OQ-364`) ·
`apps/customers/identity_match.KIND_IDENTIFIER_FIELDS` ·
`apps/customers/customer_edit.REFUSED_FIELDS` · `OQ-1241` · `OQ-1242`

## OQ-MET-12360 — what is the "contract" the new connect wizard sends the owner? (PO 2026-09-16)

**STATUS: CLOSED 2026-09-16 → the contract is a TEMPLATE, sent the way every other
letter is sent.** PO ruling, verbatim: *"using existing template and
notification"*. Nothing new is built to carry it.

**THE ANSWER, IN ONE SENTENCE.** The contract is **a document we render and
send** — one more template in the utility's own template library, merged against
the build and queued through the notification path every other letter uses. It is
**NOT** an agreement the owner signs and returns, so:

* **nothing waits for it to come back** — no new state on the connection, no
  *sent · signed · overdue*, and **no gate in front of energising a build**;
* **no file is stored** — there is nowhere for a signed copy to go and nothing
  now needs one;
* it is the **third of step 7's three messages**, beside *the build has been
  created* and *what it costs, please pay it*.

**WHY THIS WAS ASKED AT ALL, kept because the reasoning is what makes the answer
safe to build on.** Three different things are called a contract by utilities and
they cost days, weeks and nothing: a document we render; an agreement signed and
returned, which needs storage, a state and a rule about energising; or the quote
under another name. The cheap one LOOKS finished either way, which is why picking
it without a ruling was the wrong move — a utility legally required to hold a
signed copy would have discovered the gap at go-live.

**WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE BUILD.** The template picker on step 7 already exists
on the server; the notification queue already exists; `queue_document` is the
door. So the contract needs **a template row and a merge**, and no schema at all.
**Everything on step 7 is queued and nothing is sent** — this product writes a
row per message and no sender picks it up yet — and that is unchanged by this
ruling.

⚠ **IF THE PO LATER NEEDS A SIGNED COPY BACK, THAT IS A NEW RULING AND NOT AN
EXTENSION OF THIS ONE.** It would add a stored file, a state on the connection and
a decision about whether an unsigned contract stops a build energising — the third
of which is a money-and-field-work gate, not a screen change.

**Raised:** 2026-09-16 by the lane recording the PO's step-by-step walk of the new
connect wizard · **Closed:** 2026-09-16, same day, by the PO ·
**Cites:** `12-governance/02-decision-log.md` 2026-09-16 (step 7 ruling and this
closure) · `05-prototype/04 Billing, As Built.pdf` p091 (the drawn template
picker, which this ruling keeps) · `BR-MET-115` (the completion letter, moved to
the work-order screen 2026-08-25)

## OQ-BIL-12376 — does a quote hold its price between being given and being billed? (`BR-BIL-020`, 2026-09-16)

**STATUS: OPEN.** It blocks NOTHING today. The build path refuses by name when
the two figures differ, so no customer is over- or under-charged while this is
open; what the answer would change is whether that refusal becomes an automatic
choice of one figure.

**THE SITUATION, IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH REAL NUMBERS.** A developer applies to
connect twenty-five flats. On 1 August we quote them a connection fee of
**$325.00 for each of six units — $1,950.00**. On 16 September the utility puts
its connection fee up to **$340.00** on the Settings screen. On 20 September the
clerk commits the build. **Do we bill the $1,950.00 we quoted, or the $2,040.00
the price list now says?** The difference on this one line is **$90.00**.

**WHY A LANE MAY NOT SIMPLY PICK ONE.** Both answers are defensible and each
breaks something the other keeps:

* **Bill the quoted price.** Honours what the customer was told. But the quoted
  price lives in `service_request_fees.unit_amount`, and
  `customers.service_request_service.add_fee_line` takes that figure as a
  **caller-supplied argument** — so it is a free-typed amount in exactly the
  sense `BR-BIL-020` names when it says *"free-typed amounts never exist on any
  bill"*. Billing it would break the signed rule in the module that states it
  hardest.
* **Bill the catalogue price.** Obeys `BR-BIL-007` and `BR-BIL-020` exactly, one
  price list, one answer. But it means a quote is not a promise, and a customer
  who was shown a figure gets an invoice for a different one with nothing on it
  explaining why.

**WHETHER A QUOTE IS BINDING IS NOT AN ENGINEERING FACT.** It is a commercial
promise, and in some states a written quote for connection work is enforceable
for a stated period. That makes it a fact only the Product Owner holds
(CLAUDE.md law 13's third category), which is why this is asked rather than
decided.

**WHAT TO ASK THE PO.** *"We quote a developer $1,950 for six connections in
August. In September the utility raises its connection fee. When the build is
committed in September, do we bill the $1,950 we promised, or the $2,040 the new
price list says? And if we honour the old price, for how long — thirty days,
ninety, until the build commits?"*

**WHAT IS BUILT MEANWHILE, so nobody "fixes" it quietly.** Billing prices every
quote line from the tenant's own charge-code catalogue — `BR-BIL-020` obeyed —
and `metering.connections.commit_connection` compares each line's quoted unit
price against the catalogue's **before it posts anything** and refuses the whole
commit by name, printing the code and both figures. Nothing is silently chosen
and no bill is raised at a number nobody signed. **It is deliberately NOT
shipped as a quiet preference for one figure**, because either choice would be
invisible on the resulting invoice.

**Raised:** 2026-09-16 by the lane building the New Connect charges door
(`CR-109`) ·
**Cites:** `BR-BIL-020` · `BR-BIL-007` ·
`06-backend/apps/billing/fee_bill.py` (`QuotedCharge`) ·
`06-backend/apps/customers/service_request_service.py` `add_fee_line` ·
`02 Accounts Menu Blueprint.pdf` p090 · CLAUDE.md hard rule 2, law 13

## OQ-BIL-12377 — may one account carry two fee bills on the same day? (`BR-BIL-005`, 2026-09-16)

**STATUS: OPEN.** It blocks nothing in the normal case and refuses loudly in the
rare one. No money is lost either way.

**THE SITUATION, IN PLAIN ENGLISH.** A one-time bill is made idempotent by a key
built from the account, the kind of bill and its dates —
`one-time|<account>|fee|2026-09-20|2026-09-20`. That is what stops a
double-clicked button billing a customer twice, and it is the protection a clerk
most needs. **But it cannot tell two different things apart if they happen to be
the same kind, on the same account, on the same day.**

**THE CONCRETE CASE.** Balcones Development owns two sites in town. A clerk
commits the Oak Street build in the morning — six units, **$3,030.00** — and the
Pecan Street build in the afternoon — four units, **$1,860.00**. Both are `fee`
bills, both against account `A-10088`, both dated 20 September. **The second one
is refused**, naming the first run, its id, who raised it and when. The clerk can
commit it the next day and nothing is lost, but the refusal is confusing: they
did not commit the same build twice.

**WHY A LANE MAY NOT SIMPLY WIDEN THE KEY.** `core/idempotency.one_time_run_key`
is a 🔒 sensitive path (idempotency keys, CLAUDE.md), it is
`HUMAN-REVIEW-PENDING`, and its docstring says the shape *"is the only thing
decided here"*. Every one-time bill in the product — first, final, interim,
back-bill, penalty and fee — goes through it. Adding a suffix so that builds stop
colliding would change the idempotency of all six at once, which is a ruling and
not a refactor.

**WHAT TO ASK THE PO.** *"A developer with two building sites commits both on
the same day. Should the second one be allowed to raise its own bill, or is one
connection bill per customer per day the right protection against
double-clicking?"*

**WHAT IS BUILT MEANWHILE.** The existing key stands untouched and the second
commit is refused with the first run named. Nothing invents a suffix to dodge it,
and nothing silently merges two builds' charges onto one document.

**⚠ A SECOND, COMMONER CASE ARRIVED 2026-10-02 (`CR-163-BRC10` item 2, lane NC-B) —
THIS QUESTION NOW BITES ON ONE BUILD, NOT ONLY ON TWO.** A clerk can now add a fee to a
build after it was submitted, and that fee is its own new bill (an issued quote is never
edited). It is a `fee` bill against the same payer, so **a fee added on the day the build
was committed collides with the build's own quote bill and is refused.** Worked figure:
the Oak Street build is committed on 2 October with an **$800.00** quote; the clerk adds
a **$30.00** inspection fee the same afternoon and is told *"Payer already has that day's
fee. Use another posting date."*; posting it on 3 October succeeds and the build then
shows **Charged $830.00** across two bills. The dialog therefore asks for a posting date
and the refusal names the way out. Built the same way as above: the key is untouched,
nothing invents a suffix. The PO's answer to the question as put also answers this one.

**Raised:** 2026-09-16 by the lane building the New Connect charges door
(`CR-109`) ·
**Cites:** `BR-BIL-005` · `06-backend/core/idempotency.py` `one_time_run_key` ·
`06-backend/apps/billing/fee_bill.py` `raise_quote_bill` ·
CLAUDE.md 🔒 sensitive paths


## OQ-BIL-12381 — the owner pays every unit's deposit at the build: through WHICH money path? (`BR-RAT-020`/`BR-RAT-023`, 2026-09-16)

**STATUS: CLOSED 2026-09-16 — the owner pays ALL of it or NONE of it, decided once,
and a deposit NEVER moves between them.** PO verbatim: *"we can go with b - but we
need to give clark an option all or none - it means either we will charge ensite
diposte ot inwer at the time of request or we will hcharge it to tenant later - we
cannot do the transfer f depsotes later"*.

**THE ANSWER.** One flag on the build. **Owner pays** → every unit's deposit is
charged to the owner at the build and **no tenant is asked for one at move-in**.
**Tenant pays** → nothing is charged at the build and each tenant pays their own,
which is what the product does today.

**NO PER-UNIT MIX** — *"all or none"*. **AND NO TRANSFER, EVER**: this narrows the
option as it was put, which offered to release or transfer the owner's deposit as
tenants arrived. The PO refused that outright. Money held for one party does not
become money held for another because somebody moved in.

**WHERE IT SITS:** a liability at **`2300`**, never revenue at `4600`. Taking it
from the owner changes WHO we owe it to and nothing else. `BR-RAT-020` and
`BR-RAT-023` keep the amount on the plan's deposit rules and *"explicitly supersede
a flat deposit charge"*, so the owner path reads that same per-unit policy and
totals it — **it does not become a charge code on the quote.**

⚠ **THE CONSEQUENCE THAT COLLECTS TWICE IF IT IS MISSED.** Move-in must know the
deposit is already held and must not ask again. The move-in deposit step reads the
per-unit policy and would ask the tenant as a matter of course; nothing tells it
otherwise today. **The owner path is not finished when the charge posts — it is
finished when move-in can see the deposit is already held.**

⚠ **WHAT IS NOT ANSWERED AND IS NOT ASSUMED:** when the owner gets it back. With no
transfer, the deposit sits against the owner's account until something releases it.
The PO ruled how it is COLLECTED and said nothing about how it is RETURNED, and a
liability with no stated release is a balance that grows for ever. **Raised when the
path is built, not invented now.**

**Raised:** 2026-09-16 by the charges lane · **Closed:** 2026-09-16 by the PO ·
**Cites:** `BR-RAT-020` · `BR-RAT-023` · `12-governance/02-decision-log.md` 2026-09-16

## OQ-INT-12392 — Twilio call their own password an "Auth token". Do we rename it? (`CR-110-BRC04`, 2026-09-16)

**Status:** OPEN

**Who can answer it:** the Product Owner. It is a word a clerk reads on a set-up
screen, which makes it theirs (B14 rule 34 — one pair of words for one idea,
everywhere).

⚠ **AMENDED 2026-09-17 (`CR-115-BRC05`) — THIS IS NOW A TWO-VENDOR QUESTION, AND
THAT CHANGES WHAT IT IS RATHER THAN JUST ITS SIZE.** `postmark` shipped with a
field labelled **`Server token`**. Postmark scopes its credential to a *Server*
and prints *Server API Token* on the screen a clerk copies it from, so the
reasoning is identical to Twilio's and was applied identically: the box keeps
the vendor's word and the exemption list in `test_cr110_connectors.py` moved to
two entries, visibly.

**One vendor reads as a quirk; two reads as a rule that needs a stated
exception** — and a third will arrive, because *token* is simply what this
industry prints. So the question to answer is no longer *do we rename Twilio's
box* but **do we adopt a standing rule: OUR word for OUR idea is always *key*,
and a field that holds a VENDOR'S named credential keeps the vendor's own
label.** That rule, if ruled, closes this permanently and needs no revisiting
per connector. The body below is the original question and is left as written.

### The question, as it would be asked out loud

You told us to stop using two words for one thing: *"i only want to issue a key
per conenction — that waht we meant with token generation — if you want to called
it key — you can call it key — i dont understand the differnt between key and
token."* We took the word **token** off every connector screen, and it is gone
from all twenty-eight except one box.

**Twilio's own website calls their password an "Auth token".** It is the label
printed on their console, and it is what the blueprint's drawing of that screen
says too. If we rename our box to *Auth key*, a clerk who goes looking for an
*Auth key* on Twilio's site will not find one — there is no such thing there.

**So: do we keep Twilio's own word on that one box, or use ours everywhere and
accept that the label on our screen will not match the label on theirs?**

### What is built while this is open, stated so nobody "fixes" it quietly

**The box is left saying `Auth token`, exactly as the drawing shows it**, and
`test_cr110_connectors.py` **pins it by name**: the test asserts an EXACT set of
the fields on any connector whose name or label contains the word, so another
cannot appear without that list moving and a reviewer seeing it. ⚠ **That set
was `{sms_twilio · auth_token}` and became `{sms_twilio · auth_token, postmark ·
server_token}` on 2026-09-17** — the guard worked exactly as intended: it made
the lane adding Postmark come and read this question rather than type a label.

**Everything the ruling is not in doubt about IS built.** No connector asks for
a *Token address*, a token *Scope* or carries a *Generate token* button; there is
no expiry, no renewal and no re-authorise path; the whole Token panel the drawing
put on thirteen forms is gone. That is the part of the ruling nobody has to ask
about, and it is done.

⚠ **`token_exchange` is untouched and is NOT what this question is about.**
`meters_neptune360` really does swap the vendor's key for a short-lived token
when calling them, because their API demands it. That happens inside an adapter,
the word appears on no screen, and a lane must not "simplify" it away on the
strength of the ruling — the ruling is about what a clerk is asked for, not about
what an adapter does.

### Why it was not decided by us

Hard-won law 13 says a judgment call recorded with its reasoning is the
deliverable and a question is the failure to make one — and it lists what
legitimately still reaches the PO. This is on that list twice over: it is a
ruling that **collides with what is drawn**, and the collision is over a word a
clerk reads. The PO's stated reason was *our* two words for *one* idea; whether a
vendor's own product label counts as one of our words is not something a lane may
answer for them.

**Raised:** 2026-09-16 by the `CR-110-BRC04` wave C build lane ·
**Cites:** `CR-110-BRC04` · `06-backend/apps/integrations/manifests/sms_twilio.py` ·
`06-backend/tests/test_cr110_connectors.py` ·
`04-docs/05-modules/13-integrations/conformance/step0-vendors-01-10.md` (CFG-05, row 2)

## OQ-INT-12394 — the access-log panel's WATCH block is rationale, which B14 rule 33 puts at zero words on screen, and the blueprint draws it (`CR-110-BRC04`, 2026-09-16)

**Status:** OPEN

**Who can answer it:** the Product Owner. B14 rule 41 names exactly this case —
*"the only thing that reaches the PO is a drawing that contradicts a signed
rule"* — and both sides of it are theirs: the rule is one they ruled, and the
drawing is one they gave us.

### The question, as it would be asked out loud

At the bottom of *Who has been reading* — the panel that shows which partner
read what and when — there is a short note in a quote block:

> **WATCH** · Why this screen exists
> Nothing else in the product would show a partner taking two years of history
> at two in the morning.

Your own rule about screen words says a screen never explains itself to the
person reading it: *why the product works this way* belongs in the code and in
our records, not on the screen. By that rule those two lines come off.

The drawing you gave us puts them on, and that page is marked *drawn to the
rules*, so whoever drew it had already weighed the same thing and kept them.

**So: does the note stay on the screen, or come off?** Nothing else about the
panel turns on the answer — it is two lines at the foot of one panel, and taking
them off is a five-minute change either way.

### What this lane did in the meantime, and why

It **ships as drawn**, in the quieter shape the drawing gives it — a quote with
a grey left rule instead of the filled amber box that shipped before. Taking a
block the blueprint draws off the screen on a lane's own reading of rule 33
would be resolving a contradiction between two signed instructions silently, in
the direction no drawing supports. Leaving it and asking is the reversible half.

### Why it was not decided by us

Hard-won law 13 lists what legitimately reaches the PO, and *a ruling that
collides with a signed rule* is on that list — the supersession must be stated,
never assumed. Rule 33's rationale clause is the strictest sentence in B14 and
rule 41 is the newest, so a lane choosing between them is choosing which of the
PO's own instructions to break.

**Raised:** 2026-09-16 by the `CR-110-BRC04` access-log lane ·
**Cites:** `CR-110-BRC04` · `ACC-01` (Integration Blueprint p100) ·
`04-docs/02-decisions/14-ui-conventions.md` rules 33 and 41 ·
`07-frontend/src/features/integrations/AccessLogPanel.tsx` ·
`04-docs/05-modules/13-integrations/conformance/step0-connector-screens.md`

## OQ-INT-12397 — how do our `id` values travel? (`CR-111-BRC04`, 2026-09-17)

**Status:** **CLOSED 2026-09-17 — they store our text exactly as we send it.**

**PO, verbatim:** *"a) they store our text exactly as we send it"*.

### The question, as it was asked

Invoice Cloud's document prints `"id": 1001` — an integer. Ours are not integers:
an account is `A-10432` and a bill is `INV-2026-00412`. So either they store our
text, or we mint an integer for every account and every bill and keep a second
identity for ever.

### What the answer settles

**There is nothing to convert and no lookup table to keep.** `A-10432` goes out
and `A-10432` comes back. It also confirms the rule this surface already had —
B14 rule 31 and `seams/billing.as_record`'s own sentence, *"a partner keyed on our
uuid is coupled to our storage forever"* — so the NUMBER travels and the uuid
never does. Their integer samples are their examples, not a constraint.

**Built:** unchanged, which is the point — `seams/customers.as_record` and
`seams/billing.as_record` already sent our text and the divergence recorded on
`CR-110-BRC04` is now ratified rather than merely recorded.

## OQ-INT-12403 — what should `remote_plan_id` carry, and on which payloads? (`CR-111-BRC04`, 2026-09-17)

⚠ **THIS SECTION WAS `OQ-INT-12398` FOR ABOUT AN HOUR ON 2026-09-17 AND WAS
RENUMBERED.** A sibling lane pushed its own `OQ-INT-12398` (*should clearing a
non-empty address list warn first?*) between this lane's `--verify` and its
push. Both allocations were arithmetically right and both were right at the
moment they were made — which is law 11's whole point — and theirs landed
first, so this one moved. Nothing else in the repository ever cited this
number.

**Status:** **CLOSED 2026-09-17 — the account's rate plan, on `consumer-info` only.**

**PO, verbatim:** *"this rate plan ID for that account"*, and, asked back *"in
which APis is this required"*, the answer is **`consumer-info` and nowhere else** —
it appears in no other payload of their document.

### What the answer settles

An account has no plan; a **unit** does (`unit_plan_assignments`, rating-owned per
B2 r16 #6), so the read is account → unit → the assignment with no `assigned_to`.
That is the product's own precedence rather than a second opinion.

⚠ **A master account names no unit (`BR-CUS-1010`) and therefore has no plan
here, and `null` is the true answer** — an owner's account hangs off the premises
and the units below it may be on four different plans. Picking one would invent.

**Built:** `seams/customers.plan_code_map` (one query a page) and
`as_record(..., with_plan=True)`, served by `partner_consumer_info` and by no
other route. The plan's **code** travels, not its uuid — `OQ-INT-12397`'s answer
and B14 rule 31 agreeing.

## OQ-INT-12399 — what does `additional_data.payment_received` mean? (`CR-111-BRC04`, 2026-09-17)

**Status:** **OPEN.** The one of the six that was not answered.

**Who can answer it:** the Product Owner, or Invoice Cloud. It is a fact about
their document rather than about our data.

### The question, as it would be asked out loud

Their consumer record carries a field called `payment_received`. **It is a money
field and we do not know which money it means.** There are at least three
readings and they are three different numbers:

* the **last** payment's amount;
* the **total ever** received on the account;
* what was received **this billing cycle**.

For an account that has paid `$142.18` this month and `$3,410.94` since it opened,
those are `142.18`, `3410.94` and `142.18` — and the middle one is wrong by
`$3,268.76` if we guess it. A finance system reconciling against the wrong
reading balances to nothing, and nothing on either side raises.

### What is built while this is open, stated so nobody "fixes" it quietly

**The key is ABSENT from the payload — not null.** An absent key is the absence of
an answer; a null is an answer. `test_consumer_info_is_the_customers_composer_
plus_one_field` asserts `payment_received` appears nowhere in the record, so a
later lane cannot add it quietly to be helpful.

⚠ **Do NOT resolve this by picking the reading that looks most natural.** It is a
money field on a money path (prime directive), and the three readings are all
natural from where somebody is standing.

## OQ-INT-12400 — what does `projectType` say when one bill covers several services? (`CR-111-BRC04`, 2026-09-17)

**Status:** **CLOSED 2026-09-17 — always the literal `Utility Billing`.**

**PO, verbatim:** *"a) always \"Utility Billing\""*.

### What the answer settles

This product bills eleven services and routinely puts several on one document, so
*what is the type of this bill* has no single answer derived from its contents.
The ruling makes it **a fixed category on their side rather than a description of
our bill**: the same six characters on a single-service bill and on an
eleven-service one.

⚠ **WHICH MEANS IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT DERIVED, AND A LATER LANE MUST NOT
"IMPROVE" IT.** Reading the bill's services and composing *"Electric, Water"* is
the obvious next move and it is the thing that was ruled against: a partner
branching on this value would get one answer for a house on one service and
another for the house next door on two, from the same utility, on the same run.

⚠ **It is not translated.** B14 rule 35 governs what a CLERK reads in their own
language; this is a category on a partner's record in an agreed spelling, and a
localised `projectType` would be eleven values for one fact.

**Built:** `seams/billing.PROJECT_TYPE`, a module constant, on every bill record.
`test_project_type_is_a_literal_on_every_bill` pins it.

## OQ-INT-12401 — whose number does `remote_utility_id` carry in the response? (`CR-111-BRC04`, 2026-09-17)

**Status:** **CLOSED 2026-09-17 — echo back whatever they sent.**

**PO, verbatim:** *"a) echo back whatever they sent"*.

### What the answer settles

**Nothing of ours goes into it** — not the tenant id, not the subdomain, not the
utility's name. It is their own number handed back so their side can correlate a
response with the request that produced it.

⚠ **If they sent nothing the key is OMITTED, not served null.** A null would read
to their parser as *we have no id for you*, which is a statement about us; an
absent key is the absence of one.

⚠ It is also the reason this is safe: a field that echoes an input and is never
compared to anything cannot leak a utility id, which is exactly the property
`OQ-INT-12402`'s sibling ruling (*"we cannot tell tenant ID outside our system"*)
is about.

**Built:** `partner_api._echoed_utility_id` puts it in `facts` only when they sent
one; `shapes.INVOICE_CLOUD` names it in its envelope and `shapes.NATIVE` does not,
so no other partner receives the key at all.

## OQ-INT-12402 — which of Invoice Cloud's APIs do we call to collect payments, and what do they return? (`CR-111-BRC04`, 2026-09-17)

**Status:** **OPEN.**

⚠ **READ `CR-111-BRC04` §2 AND §6 FIRST — THEY CARRY THE RULING AND THIS ROW DOES
NOT REPEAT IT.** The Product Owner narrowed ruling 2 the same day it was made
(*"no this is not there - we will call htheir APis - we will ahnel those APis
seperately - rember Invoice Cloud is both direction"*): **there is no payment
file**, and `lockbox.py`, `PaymentImportBatch` and the staged-batch screen are
**not** the path here. That is recorded in the change request, in the decision
log and in `BR-INT-070`, and `OQ-INT-12396` owns the idempotency key a scheduled
pull needs. **None of it is restated here.**

### What this row adds, and it is the only thing it adds

Their document describes **no API for us to call**. So even with the transport
settled in principle, the collection cannot be written: there is no address, no
authentication shape, no payload and no paging contract for it.

**What is owed:** the endpoint(s), what one payment record carries, and how a
caller asks for a date range.

### What is built while this is open

**Nothing beyond the boundary, and no endpoint, host or payload shape is
invented** (hard-won law 3 — the unsafe option must be the one you type; an
invented SFTP path was the exact failure the earlier form of this question was
reopened to prevent).

⚠ **AND IT CANNOT BE BUILT UNTIL `DEF-INT-5574` IS RULED, WHICH IS A SEPARATE
BLOCKER AND IS NAMED HERE SO THE TWO ARE NOT CONFUSED.** A connector declares
ONE `auth.mode`, and `machine_auth._partner_manifest` issues a key only where it
reads `they_hold_ours`. *"Invoice Cloud is both direction"* is precisely the
shape a manifest cannot express today: `pay_invoicecloud` declares
`we_hold_theirs` because we hold their merchant secret to dial them, and the
partner-read half needs the opposite. **So the vendor's two halves cannot be one
connector, and the two new partner addresses cannot be switched on for the real
customer, until that is decided.**
